# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is the lecture notes of **AI618, Generative Models and Unsupervised
Learning**, a graduate course taught by Jong Chul Ye at KAIST. Every chapter
began as a scribe note written by a student who attended the lecture, and was
then merged, corrected, and edited into the chapter you are reading.

## What the course is for

Generative modelling has accumulated a great many methods in a short time, and
most treatments of it are surveys: here is a GAN, here is a VAE, here is a
diffusion model, each introduced on its own terms. The course this book comes
from is deliberately not that. It puts the emphasis on a **coherent framework
that gives a unified perspective** on the whole subject, so that the methods
appear as points in one landscape rather than as a list.

That means the mathematics is not optional background. Probability theory and
**optimal transport** are developed because they are what makes the unity
visible --- the same transport problem that defines the Wasserstein distance in
Chapter 1 returns as the Schrodinger bridge in the diffusion chapters and as
the straight-line probability path in the flow chapters. Where a method is
usually presented as a new idea, this book tries to show which older idea it is
a special case of.

The course also insists on the implementations, from classical GANs through to
diffusion and flow models, discrete diffusion, and alignment with RLHF. Where a
chapter states a result, it should also say what you would have to write down to
run it.

## How the book is organised

Five parts, following the course:

**Optimal Transport, Adversarial and Latent Variable Models.** Monge and
Kantorovich, duality, Wasserstein distances. Then GANs read through that lens
--- f-GAN, geometric GAN, W-GAN --- unpaired translation with CycleGAN and its
optimal transport form, and the StyleGAN and StarGAN families. Then the
likelihood side: the ELBO, VAE and $\beta$-VAE, normalizing flows. The part closes on
self-supervised denoising, where Tweedie's formula turns denoising into score
estimation and opens the door to everything that follows.

**Diffusion Models.** DDPM and its variational bound, score-based models
through the lens of stochastic differential equations, the probability flow
ODE. Conditioning and guidance, latent diffusion, Schrodinger bridges,
acceleration by high-order solvers and consistency models, and the applications
that made the family matter: editing, inverse problems, video and 3D.

**Flow Models.** Flow matching and its conditional form, rectified flow and
straightening, the exact relationship to diffusion, and the Kolmogorov
equations underneath both.

**Discrete Diffusion.** What has to change when the state space is categorical:
discrete flow matching, diffusion language models, the duality with the
continuous construction, and the recent large models built on it.

**Alignment with Reinforcement Learning.** RLHF, DPO and GRPO, their transfer
to diffusion and flow models, and the newer objectives that avoid trajectory
likelihoods altogether.

The through-line is worth stating once: **a score, a velocity field, and a
transport map are three ways of writing the same object.** A reader who
finishes the book should be able to move between them without thinking about
it.

## How it was made

Each lecture was written up independently by several students. Those notes
were graded against a published rubric --- coverage, technical correctness,
exposition, figures, and derivations --- with a language model producing three
independent readings per note and a human reading every one before any grade
was recorded. The model's score decided which notes were candidates for a
chapter; it never decided a grade.

Chapters are **merged, not chosen.** With only a few independent
write-ups of a lecture, the best of them still has gaps, and the grading pass
produced an explicit list of what each note was missing. The merge starts from
the strongest note and fills its gaps from the others.

## Reading this book

Chapters follow the lecture order and the parts above. Notation is consistent
within a chapter and mostly consistent across chapters; where a chapter departs
from earlier usage it says so at the start. A chapter still marked *not yet
written* is one whose scribe notes have not been merged.

The two references the course leans on throughout are Jong Chul Ye's *Geometry
of Deep Learning* (Springer, 2022) and Lipman et al., *Flow Matching Guide and
Code* ([arXiv:2412.06264](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06264)).

## Contributing

Corrections are welcome from anyone, in or out of the course. Open an issue or a
pull request. If you are reporting a mathematical error, quote the statement and
say why it is wrong --- that is more useful than a patch.
